The closure triggered significant market turmoil and widespread fears of a looming banking crisis. In response, investors sought the security of safe-haven assets. This flight to safety led to a sharp increase in the price of precious metals, with silver surging by over 5% on the following Monday, March 13, 2023. <4> On February 8, 2023, the U.S. Mint announced via the Federal Register that it was raising the retail prices on more than 20 of its 2023-dated numismatic products. [1, 2] This stronger-than-expected inflation data, with the annual rate at 6.4%, signaled persistent inflationary pressures. [3, 4] The data led investors to anticipate a more hawkish monetary policy stance from the Federal Reserve, resulting in a decline in silver prices as the market reacted to the likelihood of further interest rate hikes. [3, 7] <6> On February 1, 2023, the Institute for Supply Management (ISM) reported that its manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) for January 2023 registered 47.4%. [1, 2, 3] This marked the third consecutive month of contraction in the U.S. manufacturing sector, with the PMI reaching its lowest level since May 2020. [1, 2, 3] The report indicated that companies were slowing output to better match demand, a trend that signals a slowdown in factory activity and can influence industrial demand for commodities like silver. [1, 2, 3] <7> In early 2023, analysts predicted that silver prices could reach a nine-year high of $30 per ounce during the year. [1] This forecast was underpinned by an anticipated structural supply deficit, which, while expected to be a significant 140 million ounces, was 45% lower than the record high of 2022. The primary driver for this shortage was a projected record-breaking 8% growth in global industrial demand, expected to reach 632 million ounces. Key sectors fueling this increased demand included investments in photovoltaics, power grids, 5G networks, along with growth in consumer electronics and rising vehicle production.
